title: Overload the Java main method
answer: Yes, the `main` method can be overloaded because overloading is based on having the same method name with different parameter lists. A class can contain `main(String[] args)`, `main(int value)`, `main(String value)`, or other valid overloads. However, the Java launcher looks for the standard entry-point signature `public static void main(String[] args)` (or equivalent varargs form) when starting the class. It does not automatically choose another overloaded `main`. If you want an overload to run, the standard main method or other Java code must call it explicitly.

steps.title: Add overloaded main methods
steps.question: Java permits methods with the same name when their parameter lists differ, so overloading rules apply to `main` just as they do to other static methods. What should happen when IntelliJ adds `main(int)` and `main(String)` alongside the existing standard `main(String[])` method?
steps.why: The class should contain three valid methods named main with distinct parameter lists and no duplicate-signature conflict.

steps.title: Compile the overloads
steps.question: Overloading is a Java language feature, so the first question is whether the compiler accepts all three `main` signatures together before we discuss launcher behavior. Why should a successful `javac` compile be used to separate legal overloading from the JVM's choice of startup entry point?
steps.why: Compilation proves the overloads are legal; launch selection is a separate runtime rule.

steps.title: Launch the class normally
steps.question: The launcher invokes only the standard String-array main signature as the program entry point. The launcher chooses the standard String-array entry point rather than performing arbitrary overload resolution at startup. When `java MainMethodLab` runs even though `main(int)` and `main(String)` also exist, which overload should execute automatically and what rule explains that behavior?
steps.why: The launcher invokes only the standard String-array main signature as the program entry point.

steps.title: Separate legality from entry-point selection
steps.question: The existence of `main(int)` and `main(String)` proves that overloading is legal, but their absence from the launch output proves that startup selection follows a narrower rule. How should you explain this difference without incorrectly claiming that overloaded main methods are forbidden?
steps.why: Overloading is legal at compile time, while the launcher recognizes a specific entry-point signature at startup.
